claim: Mesenchymal stem cell (MSC) differentiation is mediated by soluble and physical cues.
source: Mesenchymal stem cell (MSC) differentiation is mediated by soluble and physical cues.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Nuclei in differentiated bovine and human MSCs stiffen and become resistant to deformation.
source: Our data show that nuclei in differentiated bovine and human MSCs stiffen and become resistant to deformation.
evidence: This claim is supported by AFM measurements and nuclear deformation assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: Attenuated nuclear deformation in differentiated MSCs is governed by restructuring of Lamin A/C and increased heterochromatin content.
source: This attenuated nuclear deformation was governed by restructuring of Lamin A/C and increased heterochromatin content.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence staining and Western blot data showing Lamin A/C reorganization and heterochromatin quantification.

claim: Change in nuclear stiffness sensitized MSCs to mechanical-loading-induced calcium signaling.
source: This change in nuclear stiffness sensitized MSCs to mechanical-loading-induced calcium signaling and differentiated marker expression.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging experiments showing increased calcium mobilization in differentiated cells upon stretch.

claim: Sensitization to mechanical loading was reversed when the 'stiff' differentiated nucleus was softened through pharmacologic treatment.
source: This sensitization was reversed when the 'stiff' differentiated nucleus was softened and was enhanced when the 'soft' undifferentiated nucleus was stiffened through pharmacologic treatment.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using TSA to soften nuclei and D-mannitol to stiffen nuclei, with corresponding calcium measurements.

claim: Dynamic loading of undifferentiated MSCs, in the absence of soluble differentiation factors, stiffened and condensed the nucleus more rapidly than soluble factors.
source: Interestingly, dynamic loading of undifferentiated MSCs, in the absence of soluble differentiation factors, stiffened and condensed the nucleus, and increased mechanosensitivity more rapidly than soluble factors.
evidence: This is supported by time-course experiments comparing dynamic loading to soluble factor treatment, showing earlier LMAC reorganization and heterochromatin formation.

claim: The nucleus acts as a mechanostat to modulate cellular mechanosensation during differentiation.
source: These data suggest that the nucleus acts as a mechanostat to modulate cellular mechanosensation during differentiation.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the collective experimental findings showing nuclear stiffness changes and altered mechanosensitivity.

claim: Physical signals from the microenvironment, including substrate stiffness, can influence MSC fate decisions.
source: While considerable work has shown the importance of soluble differentiation factors in MSC lineage specification, recent studies have also highlighted that physical signals from the microenvironment, including substrate stiffness (Engler et al., 2006), cell shape (McBeath et al., 2004), and dynamic mechanical cues (Huang et al., 2010a) can influence fate decisions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The physical properties of MSCs themselves likely change coincident with lineage specification.
source: One potentially confounding feature is that the physical properties of MSCs themselves likely change coincident with lineage specification, and such changes might alter cellular perception of super-imposed mechanical perturbations that arise from the microenvironment.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that is tested and supported by the experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Strain transfer to and deformation of the nucleus has been proposed as a direct link between mechanical inputs from the microenvironment and gene regulation.
source: Strain transfer to (and deformation of) the nucleus has been proposed as a direct link between mechanical inputs from the microenvironment and gene regulation (Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The cytoskeleton forms a mechanically continuous network within the cell and transmits extracellular mechanical signals to the nucleus through the LINC complex.
source: The cytoskeleton forms a mechanically continuous network within the cell and transmits extracellular mechanical signals from sites of matrix adhesion to the nucleus through specialized proteins that comprise the linker of nucleus and cytoskeleton (LINC) complex (Haque et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: LINC complex connections allow for direct transfer of mechanical signals to the chromatin.
source: These connections allow for direct transfer of mechanical signals to the chromatin (Wang et al., 2009; Martins et al., 2012) annscription upregulation viad can regulate intracellular signaling (Driscoll et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Chromatin remodeling induced by mechanical signals depends in part on a pre-tensed (contractile) actin cytoskeleton.
source: Chromatin remodeling induced by mechanical signals depends in part on a pre-tensed (contractile) actin cytoskeleton (Hu et al., 2005; Heo et al., 2016) and can regulate gene expression (Wang et al., 2009; Tajik et al., 2016; Shivashankar, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The nucleus is the stiffest of organelles.
source: Since the nucleus is the stiffest of organelles, changes in nuclear architecture might also impact how forces are transmitted through the cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Chromatin condensation increases nuclear stiffness.
source: It is well established that chromatin condensation increases nuclear stiffness (Dahl et al., 2005), as do changes in the amount and distribution of other intra-nuclear filamentous proteins, including the lamin protein family (Ho and Lammerding, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Nuclear lamins stabilize and stiffen the nuclear envelope and are regulated both by differentiation and the micro-elasticity of the surrounding tissue.
source: For example, nuclear lamins stabilize and stiffen the nuclear envelope and are regulated both by differentiation (Lammerding et al., 2006) and the micro-elasticity of the surrounding tissue (Swift et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mouse embryonic fibroblasts lacking lamin A/C have aberrant nuclear morphologies and exaggerated nuclear deformation in response to cell deformation.
source: Mouse embryonic fibroblasts lacking lamin A/C (LMAC) have aberrant nuclear morphologies and exaggerated nuclear deformation in response to deformation of the cell (Lammerding et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Knockdown of LMAC in the nuclei of differentiated cells decreases nuclear stiffness.
source: Knockdown of LMAC in the nuclei of differentiated cells decreases nuclear stiffness (Pajerowski et al., 2007), while overexpression in neutrophils decreases their ability to pass through micron-sized openings (Davidson et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Lamins may contribute to chromatin remodeling, gene silencing, and transcriptional activation.
source: In addition, lamins may contribute to chromatin remodeling, gene silencing, and transcriptional activation (Andrés and González, 2009; Mewborn et al., 2010) via the action of lamin binding proteins (Wilson and Foisner, 2010) and their sequestration of chromatin to the nuclear periphery (Gurudatta et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: ES cell differentiation is accompanied by an increase in chromatin condensation leading to an increase in nuclear stiffness.
source: These biophysical changes extend to the nucleus, where for instance ES cell differentiation is accompanied by an increase in chromatin condensation (Bártová et al., 2008) leading to an increase in nuclear stiffness (Pajerowski et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mouse ES cells start expressing high levels of A-type lamin during cell differentiation, suggestive of a role in the maintenance of differentiated state.
source: Lamins change during differentiation as well; mouse ES cells start expressing high levels of A-type lamin during cell differentiation, suggestive of a role in the maintenance of differentiated state.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Chromatin reorganization mediated by lamins can enhance heterochromatin formation in ES cells.
source: Further, chromatin reorganization mediated by lamins can enhance heterochromatin formation in ES cells (Galiová et al., 2008), and haplo-insufficiency of LMAC can limit certain lineages (Sehgal et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In C2C12 cells, LMAC becomes heavily concentrated at the nuclear periphery with myogenesis.
source: In C2C12 cells, a myogenic cell line, LMAC becomes heavily concentrated at the nuclear periphery with myogenesis (Markiewicz et al., 2005), and mutant isoforms of LMAC can block myogenic lineage specification (Markiewicz et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In MSCs, LMAC knockdown promotes adipocyte differentiation and decreases osteoblast differentiation.
source: In MSCs, LMAC knockdown promotes adipocyte differentiation (and decreases osteoblast differentiation) (Akter et al., 2009; Swift et al., 2013), while forced expression of the progerin mutant isoform of LMAC increases osteogenic differentiation (and reduces adipogenic differentiation) (Scaffidi and Misteli, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: When bovine MSCs were exposed to differentiation media, expression of fibrochondrogenic markers (aggrecan and collagen II) increased.
source: When bovine MSCs were exposed to differentiation media (Diff), expression of fibrochondrogenic markers (aggrecan and collagen II) increased (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a, b), consistent with previous findings (Baker and Mauck, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a, b.

claim: At early time points, stretch of the scaffold resulted in both cell and nuclear deformation in both control and differentiation conditions.
source: At early time points, stretch of the scaffold resulted in both cell and nuclear deformation, as evidenced by a marked increase in the absolute nuclear aspect ratio (NAR) values in both control (Ctrl) and differentiation (Diff) conditions (Figure 1a, c).
evidence: This claim is supported by nuclear aspect ratio measurements shown in Figure 1a, c.

claim: From day 5 onward, there was no change in the NAR in differentiated MSCs with scaffold stretch, while nuclear deformation persisted in undifferentiated MSCs.
source: From day 5 onward, however, there was no change in the NAR in differentiated MSCs (Diff) with scaffold stretch, while nuclear deformation persisted in undifferentiated MSCs (Ctrl, Figure 1b, c).
evidence: This claim is supported by nuclear aspect ratio measurements shown in Figure 1b, c.

claim: A similar reduction in nuclear deformation in response to stretch under differentiating conditions was observed in human bone marrow derived MSCs.
source: A similar effect, namely a reduction in nuclear deformation in response to stretch under differentiating conditions (Diff), was observed in both human bone marrow derived MSCs (hMSCs) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a–c) and in a human embryonic stem (ES) cell line (Figure 1—figure supplement 2d–e) treated similarly.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a–c.

claim: A similar reduction in nuclear deformation in response to stretch under differentiating conditions was observed in a human embryonic stem cell line.
source: A similar effect, namely a reduction in nuclear deformation in response to stretch under differentiating conditions (Diff), was observed in both human bone marrow derived MSCs (hMSCs) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a–c) and in a human embryonic stem (ES) cell line (Figure 1—figure supplement 2d–e) treated similarly.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2d–e.

claim: The peri-nuclear stiffness did not change for undifferentiated MSCs over seven days, but increased by >50% in differentiated MSCs.
source: Over seven days, the peri-nuclear stiffness did not change for undifferentiated MSCs (Ctrl), but increased by >50% in differentiated MSCs (Diff, Figure 2d).
evidence: This claim is supported by AFM measurements shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Treatment with CytoD did not alter peri-nuclear stiffness values, indicating that stiffening was not due to changes in f-actin organization or mechanics.
source: Treatment with CytoD (and DMSO vehicle) did not alter these values, indicating that stiffening was not due to changes in f-actin organization or mechanics, although this does not rule out potential contributions from other cytoskeletal elements (i.e. microtubules, and intermediate filaments).
evidence: This claim is supported by AFM measurements with and without CytoD treatment shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Nuclei of re-seeded differentiated MSCs did not deform when the scaffold was stretched to 10%, while re-seeded undifferentiated MSC nuclei increased in NAR by ~25%.
source: Consistent with the above findings, nuclei of these re-seeded differentiated MSCs (Diff) did not deform (Figure 2f, g) when the scaffold was stretched to 10%, while re-seeded undifferentiated MSC nuclei (Ctrl) increased in NAR by ~25%.
evidence: This claim is supported by nuclear deformation measurements shown in Figure 2f, g.

claim: Deposited extracellular matrix is not responsible for the observed attenuation in nuclear deformation with scaffold stretch.
source: These findings indicate that deposited extracellular matrix is not responsible for the observed attenuation in nuclear deformation with scaffold stretch.
evidence: This is an inference based on the re-seeding experiments showing persistent attenuation of nuclear deformation after removal of deposited matrix.

claim: Traction force increased over the first 16 hr of exposure to TGF-β3.
source: Traction force increases substantially over the first 16 hr of exposure to 10 ng/ml TGF-β3 (n = 20, Mean ± SD), where time t = 0 shows the baseline response in the absence of TGF-β3.
evidence: This claim is supported by traction force measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: MSCs cultured in Diff conditions for 7 days showed significant post deflections compared to MSCs in Ctrl conditions.
source: Micro-Post Array Detector (mPAD) analysis showed little post deflection by MSCs in Ctrl conditions, while MSCs cultured in Diff conditions for 7 days showed significant post deflections (bar = 30 μm, F-actin: green; nuclei: blue) and quantification (c) showed that strain energy per cell was higher in MSCs in Diff conditions compared to MSCs in Ctrl conditions (Student's t-test, *p<0.0001 vs. Ctrl, n = 20/condition, Mean ± SEM).
evidence: This claim is supported by mPAD analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b, c.

claim: Blockade of acto-myosin contractility decreased nuclear deformation in undifferentiated cells.
source: On scaffolds, blockade of acto-myosin contractility decreased nuclear deformation in undifferentiated cells (Ctrl/Y27, Figure 2—figure supplement 1d), implicating the need for a patent and contractile cytoskeleton in the transfer of deformation from the scaffold to the nucleus.
evidence: This claim is supported by nuclear deformation measurements with ROCK inhibition shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Nuclear stiffening with differentiation dominates the response, resulting in a nucleus that no longer deforms when the cell is stretched.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that nuclear stiffening with differentiation dominates the response, resulting in a nucleus that no longer deforms when the cell is stretched.
evidence: This is an inference based on the collective experimental findings.

claim: On day 1, LMAC was distributed throughout the MSC nucleus, and in Ctrl conditions, this distribution did not change through day 7.
source: On day 1, LMAC was distributed throughout the MSC nucleus (Figure 3a), and in Ctrl conditions, this distribution did not change through day 7 (Figure 3a and Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 3a and Video 1.

claim: Under Diff conditions, LMAC remodeled to localize solely to the nuclear periphery.
source: Under Diff conditions, LMAC remodeled to localize solely to the nuclear periphery (Figure 3a, b and Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 3a, b and Video 2.

claim: Localization of LMAC to the nuclear periphery was accompanied by a ~50% increase in A-type lamin protein content.
source: Localization to the nuclear periphery was accompanied by a ~50% increase in A-type lamin protein content (Figure 3c, d).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 3c, d.

claim: Staining for H3K27me3 revealed a marked increase in the number of heterochromatin-rich nodules throughout the nucleus with differentiation.
source: Likewise, staining for H3K27me3 (a heterochromatin marker) revealed a marked increase in the number of heterochromatin-rich nodules throughout the nucleus with differentiation (Diff, p<0.05 vs. Ctrl, Figure 3e, f).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 3e, f.

claim: Treatment of differentiated cells with TSA for 24 hr induces chromatin relaxation and resulted in a marked reduction in both heterochromatin content and nuclear stiffness.
source: Treatment of differentiated cells with TSA for 24 hr induces chromatin relaxation and, in this study, resulted in a marked reduction in both heterochromatin content and nuclear stiffness (Diff/TSA, Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, b and Figure 4—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: This claim is supported by heterochromatin staining and AFM measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, b, f.

claim: TSA did not alter the distribution or the amount of LMAC in differentiated cells.
source: While TSA did not alter the distribution or the amount of LMAC in these differentiated cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c–e), it did partially restore nuclear deformation in response to scaffold stretch (Figure 4a, b).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c–e.

claim: TSA partially restored nuclear deformation in response to scaffold stretch in differentiated cells.
source: While TSA did not alter the distribution or the amount of LMAC in these differentiated cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c–e), it did partially restore nuclear deformation in response to scaffold stretch (Figure 4a, b).
evidence: This claim is supported by nuclear deformation measurements shown in Figure 4a, b.

claim: In undifferentiated MSCs, a rapid stretch resulted in a small increase in intracellular Ca2+, while in differentiated MSCs, a much larger increase was observed.
source: In undifferentiated MSCs (Ctrl), a rapid stretch resulted in a small increase in intracellular Ca2+. When the same perturbation was applied to differentiated MSCs (Diff), a much larger increase was observed (p<0.01, Figure 4c, i).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4c, i.

claim: The enhanced sensitivity to mechanical perturbation in differentiated MSCs was reversed by pre-treatment with TSA.
source: Interestingly, this enhanced sensitivity was reversed by pre-treatment of differentiated MSCs with TSA (Diff/TSA).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data showing reduced calcium response in TSA-treated differentiated cells.

claim: Sensitization to mechanical perturbation with differentiation and blockade with TSA treatment was also observed for aggrecan and collagen II gene expression.
source: This sensitization to mechanical perturbation with differentiation (and blockade with TSA treatment) was also observed for aggrecan and collagen II gene expression (Figure 4d, e).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4d, e.

claim: With TSA pre-treatment, there were no significant changes in cytoskeletal structure, contractility, or migration rate.
source: With TSA pre-treatment (Diff/TSA), we found no significant changes in cytoskeletal structure, contractility (as assessed by myosin light chain phosphorylation, pMLCK) or migration rate (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a–e).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2a–e.

claim: Pre-treatment of MSCs with D-mannitol decreased nuclear deformation with stretch.
source: To test the converse, undifferentiated MSCs were transiently exposed to a hypertonic solution [500 mM D-mannitol (DM), (Irianto et al., 2013), Ctrl/DM] for 30 min, which has been shown to induce the rapid condensation of nuclear chromatin. This treatment resulted in MSC nuclei that were more resistant to deformation when the scaffold was deformed (Figure 4—figure supplement 2f–g, Figure 4f–g).
evidence: This claim is supported by nuclear deformation measurements shown in Figure 4f–g and Figure 4—figure supplement 2f–g.

claim: D-mannitol treatment did not alter the organization of the actin cytoskeleton.
source: Importantly, this treatment (Ctrl/DM) did not alter the organization of the actin cytoskeleton (Figure 4—figure supplement 2h).
evidence: This claim is supported by phalloidin staining shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2h.

claim: When stretch was applied to MSCs whose nuclei were artificially stiffer, a marked increase in calcium mobilization was observed.
source: When stretch was applied to MSCs whose nuclei were artificially stiffer, but still undifferentiated, a marked increase in calcium mobilization was once again observed (Figure 4h, i).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4h, i.

claim: Short periods of dynamic loading (1 hr of dynamic stretch per day for 5 days) did not alter LMAC distribution.
source: These studies showed that short periods of dynamic loading [1 hr of dynamic stretch (3%, 1 Hz)] that was applied each day for 5 days did not alter LMAC distribution (Figure 5a, b).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 5a, b.

claim: When dynamic loading was applied for 3 or 6 hr per day, LMAC reorganization was evident by day 5.
source: However, when the same loading regimen was applied for 3 or 6 hr per day, LMAC reorganization was evident by day 5 (Figure 5c, d; Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 5c, d and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: LMAC reorganization was evident with 1.5% and 3% stretch, but not at 0.75% stretch.
source: Strain magnitude also modulated this process; LMAC reorganization was evident with 1.5% and 3% stretch, but not at 0.75% stretch (applied for 6 hr per day, Figure 5d–g, Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 5d–g and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: LMAC staining intensity and organization in mechanically pre-conditioned MSCs was similar to that observed in MSCs differentiated via soluble mediators.
source: LMAC staining intensity and organization in these mechanically pre-conditioned MSCs (i.e. those exposed to higher levels of DL for longer periods of time) was similar to that observed in MSCs differentiated via soluble mediators (Diff, Figure 5—figure supplement 1c), suggesting that LMAC reorganization mediated through mechanical signals matches or exceeds that of soluble-factor-mediated differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Dynamic loading conditions led to a marked increase in heterochromatin content, comparable to that induced by soluble factors.
source: Similarly, dynamic loading (DL) conditions led to a marked increase in heterochromatin content, comparable to that induced by soluble factors (Figure 5—figure supplement 1d, e).
evidence: This claim is supported by heterochromatin staining shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1d, e.

claim: When mechanically pre-conditioned MSCs were reseeded onto new scaffolds, nuclear deformation with 10% scaffold stretch was lower than for undifferentiated MSCs, approaching the levels observed in MSCs differentiated via soluble mediators.
source: When mechanically pre-conditioned MSCs (DL, 3%, 1 Hz, 6 hr, 5 days of loading) were reseeded onto new scaffolds, nuclear deformation with 10% scaffold stretch was lower than for undifferentiated MSCs, approaching the levels observed in MSCs differentiated via soluble mediators (Diff, Figure 5h).
evidence: This claim is supported by nuclear deformation measurements shown in Figure 5h.

claim: Nuclei in DL pre-conditioned cells were stiffer than undifferentiated MSCs, although not as stiff as nuclei in MSCs differentiated via soluble factors.
source: Nuclei in DL pre-conditioned cells were stiffer than undifferentiated MSCs, although not as stiff as nuclei in MSCs differentiated via soluble factors (Diff, Figure 5i).
evidence: This claim is supported by AFM measurements shown in Figure 5i.

claim: DL increased aggrecan and TGF-β gene expression to levels higher than in differentiation conditions.
source: Furthermore, DL increased aggrecan (AGG) and TGF-β gene expression to levels higher than in differentiation conditions (Diff, Figure 5j, k).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5j, k.

claim: Addition of low levels of exogenous TGF-β3 (1 ng/mL) for 1 week resulted in changes in LMAC distribution and increases in heterochromatin in MSCs.
source: Indeed, addition of low levels of exogenous TGF-β3 (1 ng/mL) for 1 week resulted in changes in LMAC distribution and increases in heterochromatin in MSCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1f.

claim: When a rapid stretch was applied to DL pre-conditioned MSCs, a greater increase in intracellular calcium was observed, compared to undifferentiated MSCs.
source: When a rapid stretch was applied to DL pre-conditioned MSCs, a greater increase in intracellular calcium was observed, compared to undifferentiated MSCs (ctrl, Figure 5l).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5l.

claim: Mechanical stimulation can drive lineage specification, including alterations in nuclear organization and mechanics.
source: Overall, these data suggest that mechanical stimulation can drive lineage specification, including alterations in nuclear organization and mechanics, and that these changes may be mediated through autocrine/paracrine signaling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the collective experimental findings showing mechanical loading effects.

claim: Dynamic loading alone can produce a mechanically-preconditioned nuclear state that is similar (but distinct) to that brought about by soluble factors.
source: Importantly, in the absence of exogenous differentiation factors, dynamic loading alone can produce a mechanically-preconditioned nuclear state that is similar (but distinct) to that brought about by soluble factors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of dynamic loading and soluble factor effects on nuclear properties.

claim: TGF-β3 did not alter LMAC organization or gene expression over the first 3 days of culture.
source: TGF-β3 (Diff) did not alter LAMC organization or gene expression over the first 3 days of culture (Figure 6a, d).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and gene expression data shown in Figure 6a, d.

claim: Within just 2 days under DL conditions, reorganization of LMAC was already apparent, with translocation to the nuclear envelope complete by day 3.
source: However, within just 2 days under DL conditions, reorganization of LMAC was already apparent, with translocation to the nuclear envelope complete by day 3 (Figure 6a) and increased LMAC gene expression with DL at each time point (Figure 6d).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and gene expression data shown in Figure 6a, d.

claim: HTC staining intensified more rapidly under DL conditions compared to Diff, with a higher number of heterochromatin-rich nodules present as early as day 1.
source: Interestingly, HTC staining intensified more rapidly under DL conditions compared to Diff, with a higher number of heterochromatin-rich nodules present as early as day 1 (compared to day 3 under Diff conditions, Figure 6b, c).
evidence: This claim is supported by heterochromatin staining shown in Figure 6b, c.

claim: Chromatin condensation parameter analysis showed a more rapid structural reorganization of the nucleus under DL conditions, compared to culture in differentiation medium.
source: This quantitative analysis showed a more rapid structural reorganization of the nucleus under DL conditions, compared to culture in differentiation medium (Figure 6e, f).
evidence: This claim is supported by chromatin condensation parameter analysis shown in Figure 6e, f.

claim: Gene expression analysis revealed an early and robust response to dynamic loading in comparison to the addition of exogenous TGF-β3.
source: Along with this, gene expression analysis revealed an early and robust response to dynamic loading in comparison to the addition of exogenous TGF-β3 (Diff, Figure 6—figure supplement 1a–d).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a–d.

claim: The nucleus acts as a mechanical rheostat within progenitor cells, where increases in nuclear stiffness sensitize the entire transduction machinery to prime the cell response to mechanical perturbation.
source: In addition to being the site for storage of genetic material and gene transcription, the nucleus, which is generally the stiffest element of all eukaryotic cells (Dahl et al., 2008), plays a central role in mechanical strain transduction from the external microenvironment. While the mechanisms by which nuclear deformation regulates transcriptional activities are only now beginning to be elucidated, our data suggest that the nucleus acts as a mechanical rheostat within progenitor cells, where increases in nuclear stiffness sensitize the entire transduction machinery to prime the cell response to mechanical perturbation.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the collective experimental findings.

claim: Soluble differentiation factors and mechanical perturbation elicit marked changes in nuclear deformability, stiffness and organization as a direct consequence of chromatin condensation and restructuring of the Lamin A/C network.
source: Our data show that soluble differentiation factors as well as mechanical perturbation on its own, elicit marked changes in nuclear deformability, stiffness and organization as a direct consequence of chromatin condensation and restructuring of the Lamin A/C network in both adult progenitor cells and in embryonic stem cells.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Change in nuclear mechanics and organization led to a greater mobilization of intracellular calcium when pre-conditioned mesenchymal stem cells were exposed to stretch.
source: This change in nuclear mechanics and organization led to a greater mobilization of intracellular calcium when pre-conditioned mesenchymal stem cells were exposed to stretch, likely as a consequence of the nucleus transforming from a strain sink (an object that readily deforms) to a strain concentrator (an object that stops deforming, forcing other components to deform more).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging experiments and is an inference about the mechanism.

claim: The nucleus transforms from a strain sink to a strain concentrator with differentiation.
source: This change in nuclear mechanics and organization led to a greater mobilization of intracellular calcium when pre-conditioned mesenchymal stem cells were exposed to stretch, likely as a consequence of the nucleus transforming from a strain sink (an object that readily deforms) to a strain concentrator (an object that stops deforming, forcing other components to deform more).
evidence: This is an interpretive model based on the experimental findings.

claim: When one element of an elastic mechanical linkage stiffens, the other weaker elements must deform more when the system is elongated by a set amount.
source: When one element of an elastic mechanical linkage stiffens, the other weaker elements must deform more when the system is elongated by a set amount.
evidence: This is a statement based on mechanical principles.

claim: The stiffness of native tissue extracellular matrices defines the resting levels and ratios of Lamin isoforms in adult cells, with stiffer microenvironments increasing nuclear mechanics.
source: Swift and colleagues recently showed that the stiffness of native tissue extracellular matrices defines the resting levels and ratios of Lamin isoforms in adult cells, with stiffer microenvironments increasing nuclear mechanics (Swift et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Dynamic mechanical forces transmitted through the environment may continuously adjust nuclear mechanics to modulate progenitor cell mechanosensitivity during tissue formation and repair.
source: Thus, dynamic mechanical forces transmitted through the environment may continuously adjust nuclear mechanics to modulate progenitor cell mechanosensitivity during tissue formation and repair.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings and their implications.

claim: Both BMP and TGF-β signaling increase baseline cellular contractility.
source: For example, both BMP and TGF-β signaling increase baseline cellular contractility (Bhadriraju et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: TGF-β expression is highly upregulated with dynamic stretch at early time points.
source: Our data show that TGF-β expression is highly upregulated with dynamic stretch at early time points and while TGF-β in the media did not reach detectable levels, we did observe increased Smad3 signaling in response to stretch (Figure 6—figure supplement 1e, [Furumatsu et al., 2013; Li et al., 2015]).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data and Western blot analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1e.

claim: Mechanical perturbation itself can increase cell contractility and spreading.
source: Mechanical perturbation itself can also increase cell contractility and spreading (Cui et al., 2015), and influence the subsequent mechano-response.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Artificially increasing Rho GTPase activity in endothelial cells sensitizes their response to applied stretch.
source: Kaunas et al. showed that artificially increasing Rho GTPase activity in endothelial cells sensitizes their response to applied stretch (Kaunas et al., 2005), and Deguchi et al. showed that fluid shear stress, which also increases contractility, can stiffen the endothelial cell nucleus (Deguchi et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Local application of mechanical force to the apical surface of cells causes local chromatin reorganization.
source: Recent work by the Shivashankar and Burridge groups has shown that local application of mechanical force to the apical surface of cells causes local chromatin reorganization (Iyer et al., 2012) and that pulling on isolated nuclei results in changes in Lamin organization and nuclear stiffening (Guilluy et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The stiffer nucleus of differentiated cells can act as a stress concentrator, sensitizing these cells to mobilize calcium to a greater extent when external deformation is applied.
source: Regardless of the path to nuclear reorganization, our data provide evidence that the stiffer nucleus of differentiated cells can act as a stress concentrator (Figure 7), sensitizing these cells to mobilize calcium to a greater extent when external deformation is applied.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the experimental findings, illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Increased calcium mobilization may itself impact lamin processing, creating a feed-forward loop to ensure that the nucleus remains patent under conditions of high mechanical activity.
source: This increased calcium mobilization may itself impact lamin processing (Kalinowski et al., 2013), creating a feed-forward loop to ensure that the nucleus remains patent under conditions of high mechanical activity.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on citation to prior work and the current findings.

claim: ATP-purinergic signaling is a central modulator in the load-induced-chromatin condensation in MSCs.
source: We recently showed that ATP-purinergic signaling is a central modulator in the load-induced-chromatin condensation in MSCs, as is signaling thorough Smad proteins (Heo et al., 2015, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: The giant isoform of nesprin-1 is essential for mechanical force transfer to the nucleus and activation of the YAP/TAZ pathway in response to exogenous mechanical loading.
source: Further, we have established that the giant isoform of nesprin-1 (a component of the LINC complex that mediates actin connectivity to the nucleus) is essential for mechanical force transfer to the nucleus and activation of the YAP/TAZ pathway in response to exogenous mechanical loading (Driscoll et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Both mechanical forces and soluble factors had similar effects on nuclear properties and reorganization, but those mediated by soluble factor addition arose more slowly than those wrought by mechanical forces.
source: While both mechanical forces and soluble factors had similar effects on nuclear properties and reorganization, those mediated by soluble factor addition arose more slowly than those wrought by mechanical forces.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the time-course experiments comparing dynamic loading and soluble factor treatment.

claim: The mechanical environment plays a significant role in dynamically modulating nuclear properties.
source: This suggests that the mechanical environment plays a significant role in dynamically modulating nuclear properties.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that mechanical forces act more rapidly than soluble factors.

claim: As MSCs transit between phenotypes, their current differentiation status and time history of exposure to soluble or mechanical factors could influence their mechanobiologic response upon implantation.
source: That is, as MSCs transit between phenotypes, one would expect that their current differentiation status and time history of exposure to soluble or mechanical factors could influence their mechanobiologic response upon implantation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the implications of the findings for therapeutic applications.

claim: Soluble factors resulted in complete abrogation of nuclear deformation, while mechanically mediated reorganization of the nucleus resulted in only a diminution of nuclear deformation with stretch.
source: In addition to material design, we also noted a path-dependent aspect in terms of the end results of nuclear reorganization; soluble factors resulted in complete abrogation of nuclear deformation, while mechanically mediated reorganization of the nucleus resulted in only a diminution of nuclear deformation with stretch.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the comparison of nuclear deformation in cells treated with soluble factors versus dynamic loading.

claim: If nuclear deformation is essential for physiologic function, then complete elimination of nuclear deformation may result in aberrant mechano-signaling.
source: If nuclear deformation is essential for physiologic function, then complete elimination of nuclear deformation (as a consequence of soluble factor addition) may result in aberrant mechano-signaling.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential consequences of the findings.

claim: The data demonstrates a mechanism whereby nuclear architecture and stiffness can be tuned to dynamically regulate cellular mechanosensitivity to promote and preserve lineage specification.
source: In conclusion, the data presented herein demonstrates a mechanism whereby nuclear architecture and stiffness can be tuned to dynamically regulate cellular mechanosensitivity to promote and preserve lineage specification.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the collective experimental findings.

claim: Aligned nanofibrous scaffolds direct new tissue formation for fibrous tissue engineering.
source: Specifically, we examined the nuclear mechanics and mechanosensitivity of MSCs as they transited toward a differentiated (fibrochondrogenic) lineage on aligned nanofibrous scaffolds. These scaffolds not only direct new tissue formation for fibrous tissue engineering (Nerurkar et al., 2009; Baker et al., 2012) but also provide a useful template for the application of coordinated cell deformation (Nathan et al., 2011; Heo et al., 2011; Han et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: MSC fibrochondrogenesis mediated by soluble factor addition over the long term increases nuclear stiffness and alters organization of key nuclear structural elements.
source: Using this experimental platform, we show that MSC fibrochondrogenesis mediated by soluble factor addition over the long term (days to weeks) increases nuclear stiffness, alters organization of key nuclear structural elements, and as a consequence, changes the manner in which MSCs respond in the short term (seconds to minutes) to dynamic mechanical signals from the microenvironment.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: Repeated application of short term dynamic mechanical stimulation can evoke changes in nuclear structure and mechanics more rapidly than soluble factor addition alone.
source: We further demonstrate that the repeated application of this short term dynamic mechanical stimulation (as opposed to application of soluble differentiation factors) can itself evoke some of these same changes in nuclear structure and mechanics, and that it does so more rapidly than soluble factor addition alone.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: Nuclear stiffening may be both a consequence and mediator of differentiation, tuning how progenitor cells interpret mechanical cues from their microenvironment.
source: This implies that nuclear stiffening may be both a consequence and mediator of differentiation, tuning how progenitor cells interpret mechanical cues from their microenvironment.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Changes in nuclear stiffness may act to first inform, and then reinforce, signals that promote and preserve lineage specification.
source: Such changes may act to first inform, and then reinforce, signals that promote and preserve lineage specification.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion about the functional significance of the findings.
